title: The Secret History of the Antichrist
description:
in History, Religion |   	August 18th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Pay­Pal co-founder Peter Thiel has spo­ken pub­licly on a vari­ety of issues
body:
in History, Religion |   	August 18th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Pay­Pal co-founder Peter Thiel has spo­ken pub­licly on a vari­ety of issues from con­trar­i­an entre­pre­neur­ship to tech­ni­cal stag­na­tion to geopo­lit­i­cal strug­gle. Late­ly, he’s drawn more atten­tion with extend­ed remarks on what would seem an unex­pect­ed sub­ject: the Antichrist, a seem­ing­ly enlight­ened but decep­tive­ly malev­o­lent fig­ure or move­ment bent on putting the world under inno­va­tion-sti­fling uni­fied con­trol. The term itself may sound famil­iar, though many of us haven’t seen it ref­er­enced much in pop­u­lar cul­ture since the hey­day of the Left Behind nov­el series that sold so well around the turn of the mil­len­ni­um. Whether or not it’s to your lit­er­ary taste, that apoc­a­lypse nar­ra­tive’s vil­lain does adhere to the Antichrist arche­type laid out in the Bible.
In the new Hochela­ga video above, Tom­mie Trelawny goes back to the bib­li­cal texts to deter­mine the ori­gins of the Antichrist, whom human­i­ty has por­trayed as “a great deceiv­er who charms the world through false mir­a­cles, and with it, demands to be wor­shiped as god him­self.” How­ev­er large he looms in mod­ern Chris­t­ian sto­ry­telling, he’s ref­er­enced in only four pas­sages of the Bible. The word Antichrist appears nowhere but in one of John’s epis­tles, which also warns that “even now many antichrists have come,” indi­cat­ing, as Trelawny puts it, those who reject “that Jesus is the Christ, or Mes­si­ah.” As John saw it, some such indi­vid­u­als — includ­ing mem­bers of new sects like Gnos­ti­cism — were also dan­ger­ous­ly charis­mat­ic, which aid­ed the spread of their false doc­trines.
The apos­tle Paul or one of his dis­ci­ples, in a let­ter to the Thes­sa­lo­ni­ans, fore­sees the rise of “a mys­te­ri­ous fig­ure known only as ‘the law­less one,’ who will gain pow­er by deceiv­ing peo­ple through false mir­a­cles, and once in pow­er, he will com­mit his great­est crime of all: ‘He will oppose and exalt him­self over every­thing that is called God or wor­shiped, so that he sets him­self up in God’s tem­ple, pro­claim­ing him­self to be God.” For its part, the Book of Rev­e­la­tion adds “the arrival of a mon­strous sev­en-head­ed beast,” and lat­er, a com­pan­ion with “the horns of a lamb but the voice of a drag­on.” There­after comes the “mark of the beast,” 666 — or per­haps 616, Trelawny adds, giv­en that either could be seen as code for Neron Kaisar in Greek or Nero Cae­sar in Latin, bet­ter known as the ancient Roman Emper­or Nero. Some sus­pect­ed him of being the Antichrist, espe­cial­ly if he orches­trat­ed Rome’s great fire in order to con­sol­i­date his pow­er and scape­goat the Chris­tians.
Trelawny also gets into detail about the twice-excom­mu­ni­cat­ed Holy Roman Emper­or Fred­er­ick II, whom Pope Gre­go­ry IX saw as the proph­e­sied “law­less one,” and even into the accu­sa­tions of being the Antichrist flung back and forth dur­ing the Protes­tant Ref­or­ma­tion and the flur­ry of print­ed pam­phlets that drove its sur­round­ing con­tro­ver­sy. The lat­ter sto­ry “shows a sub­tle change tak­ing place in how peo­ple could under­stand the Antichrist. It was no longer just a sin­gle per­son; it could be an entire sys­tem or insti­tu­tion.” Through­out his­to­ry, as under­scored today by anony­mous online debates as well as lec­tures deliv­ered by Peter Thiel in Rome, “it seems that what­ev­er peo­ple fear the most, from com­mu­nism to glob­al­ism to reg­u­la­tion, the Antichrist can become.” If so, we’ll keep hear­ing about his immi­nent (or already accom­plished) rise until human­i­ty can get over its fears — and what a mir­a­cle that would be.

title: NASA Enlists Andy Warhol, Annie Leibovitz, Norman Rockwell & 350 Other Artists to Visually Document America’s Space Program
description:
in Art, Astronomy, History, Science, Technology |   	August 19th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			
It’s hard to imag­ine that the space-crazed gen­er­al
body:
in Art, Astronomy, History, Science, Technology |   	August 19th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			
It’s hard to imag­ine that the space-crazed gen­er­al pub­lic need­ed any help get­ting worked up about astro­nauts and NASA in the ear­ly ’60s.
Per­haps the wild pop­u­lar­i­ty of space-relat­ed imagery was in part what moti­vat­ed NASA admin­is­tra­tor James Webb to cre­ate the NASA Art Pro­gram in 1962.

Although the pro­gram’s hand­picked artists weren’t edit­ed or cen­sored in any way, they were briefed on how NASA hoped to be rep­re­sent­ed, and which emo­tions their cre­ations were meant to capture—the excite­ment and uncer­tain­ty of explor­ing these fron­tiers.
NASA was also care­ful to col­lect every­thing the artists pro­duced while par­tic­i­pat­ing in the pro­gram, from sketch­es to fin­ished work.
In turn, the artists received unprece­dent­ed access to launch sites, key per­son­nel, and major events such as Project Mer­cury and the Apol­lo 11 Mis­sion.
Hun­dreds of artists, includ­ing Andy Warhol, Nor­man Rock­well, and Lau­rie Ander­son, have brought their unique sen­si­bil­i­ties to the project. (Find NASA-inspired art by Warhol and Rock­well above.)
(And hey, no shame if you mis­tak­en­ly assumed Warhol’s 1987 Moon­walk 1 was cre­at­ed as a pro­mo for MTV…)

Jamie Wyeth’s 1964 water­col­or Gem­i­ni Launch Pad includes a hum­ble bicy­cle, the means by which tech­ni­cians trav­eled back and forth between the launch pad and the rein­forced-con­crete block­house where they worked.


Pho­tog­ra­ph­er Annie Lei­bovitz offers two views of NASA’s first female pilot and com­man­der, Eileen Collins—with and with­out hel­met.

Postage stamp design­er, Paul Calle, one of the inau­gur­al group of par­tic­i­pat­ing artists, pro­duced a stamp com­mem­o­rat­ing the Gem­i­ni 4 space cap­sule in cel­e­bra­tion of NASA’s 9th anniver­sary. When the Apol­lo 11 astro­nauts suit­ed up pri­or to blastoff on July 16, 1969, Calle was the only artist present. His quick­ly ren­dered felt-tip mark­er sketch­es lend a back­stage ele­ment to the hero­ic iconog­ra­phy sur­round­ing astro­nauts Arm­strong, Aldrin and Collins. One of the items they car­ried with them on their jour­ney was the engraved print­ing plate of Calle’s 1967 com­mem­o­ra­tive stamp. They hand-can­celed a proof aboard the flight, on the assump­tion that post offices might be hard to come by on the moon.

In 2016, NASA’s Jet Propul­sion Lab­o­ra­to­ry enlist­ed a team of nine artists, design­ers, and illus­tra­tors to col­lab­o­rate on 14 posters, a visu­al throw­back to the ones the WPA cre­at­ed between 1938 and 1941 to spark pub­lic inter­est in the Nation­al Parks. You can see the results at the Exo­plan­et Trav­el Bureau.
More recent­ly, in 2024, NASA and the artist team Ger­aluz and WERC relaunched the pro­gram with space-themed murals in Man­hat­tan.
View an album of 25 his­toric works from NASA’s Art Pro­gram here.
Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2019.

title: The Complete History of the Beatles as Told By Conan O’Brien
description:
in History, Music |   	August 19th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

The world end­ed in the nine­teen-six­ties. Or rather, one world end­ed in the n
body:
in History, Music |   	August 19th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

The world end­ed in the nine­teen-six­ties. Or rather, one world end­ed in the nine­teen-six­ties and gave way to anoth­er, a tran­si­tion per­son­i­fied by no human beings more clear­ly than the Bea­t­les. “They are light­ning rods for so much that makes the six­ties a rev­o­lu­tion­ary decade,” says The Rest Is His­to­ry pod­cast co-host Tom Hol­land in the video above. “In all kinds of ways, in the twen­ty-first cen­tu­ry, we’re liv­ing in the after­math of what hap­pened in the six­ties, rather like peo­ple in the six­teenth cen­tu­ry were liv­ing in the after­math of what hap­pened in the fif­teen-twen­ties.” Many of the show’s reg­u­lar lis­ten­ers will grasp that anal­o­gy imme­di­ate­ly, though per­haps few­er of those who’ve tuned in to this espe­cial­ly pop­u­lar episode, in which Hol­land recounts the com­plete his­to­ry of the Bea­t­les with Conan O’Brien.


	

O’Brien has nev­er made a secret of his Bea­t­les obses­sion, but here he demon­strates it defin­i­tive­ly by sup­ply­ing most of the details of the band’s sto­ry him­self. (That goes even for rel­a­tive­ly obscure ones: he men­tions, for exam­ple, the score Paul McCart­ney com­posed for the film The Fam­i­ly Way, fea­tured ear­li­er this year on Open Cul­ture.) He also man­ages to win the triv­ia con­test against Hol­land at Abbey Road Stu­dios in the video just above, but then, he’d been study­ing in one sense or anoth­er for quite some time. A decade ago, he held his own in con­ver­sa­tion with Mark Lewisohn, the first vol­ume of whose painstak­ing three-part Bea­t­les biog­ra­phy comes to near­ly a thou­sand pages in the abridged edi­tion. That was on his YouTube inter­view series Seri­ous Jib­ber-Jab­ber, the pre­de­ces­sor to his cur­rent pod­cast Conan O’Brien Needs a Friend.
Hol­land and his co-host Dominic Sand­brook appeared on Conan O’Brien Needs a Friend last fall. They may have seemed an odd choice in a guest ros­ter con­sist­ing most­ly of come­di­ans, actors, and musi­cians, but O’Brien him­self has declared The Rest Is His­to­ry “the best pod­cast in the world,” and their shows’ fan bases turn out not to be mutu­al­ly exclu­sive. That wide-rang­ing con­ver­sa­tion went stim­u­lat­ing­ly enough to inspire a com­ple­tion of the crossover just a few months there­after, when Hol­land brought O’Brien to Abbey Road for an hour and a half of noth­ing but talk about the his­tor­i­cal sig­nif­i­cance of the Bea­t­les, whom O’Brien declares “a com­plete break from what hap­pened before.” (Sand­brook, the rare non-appre­ci­a­tor of the Fab Four, absent­ed him­self from the dis­cus­sion.)


	

O’Brien prais­es books like Lewisohn’s, as well as Ian Leslie’s more recent John & Paul: A Love Sto­ry in Songs, but his under­stand­ing of the group as a his­tor­i­cal phe­nom­e­non sug­gests that he’s also read the work of crit­ic Ian Mac­Don­ald. After Revolver, “it seemed to West­ern youth that The Bea­t­les knew — that they had the key to cur­rent events and were some­how orches­trat­ing them through their records.” So Mac­Don­ald writes in his book Rev­o­lu­tion in the Head: The Bea­t­les’ Records and the Six­ties, whose title refers to “the true rev­o­lu­tion of the Six­ties”: an uncon­scious men­tal adap­ta­tion to the pas­sage from a local real­i­ty of “con­sen­sus, hier­ar­chy, and fixed val­ues” to a glob­al one of indi­vid­u­al­ism, sen­sa­tion­al­ism, and “jeal­ous­ly lev­eled stan­dards.” The Bea­t­les did­n’t cause those changes, as they them­selves well under­stood. But they accept­ed the roles of its avatars, and more than 60 years after the rise of Beat­le­ma­nia, we still live in the world they rep­re­sent­ed.

title: 5,000 Classic Movie Posters Digitized & Put Online: Free to Browse & Download
description: Who hasn’t pinned one of Saul Bass’ ele­gant film posters on their wall—either with thumb­tacks above the dorm room bed or in frame and glass in
body:
Who hasn’t pinned one of Saul Bass’ ele­gant film posters on their wall—either with thumb­tacks above the dorm room bed or in frame and glass in grown-up envi­rons? Or maybe it’s 70s kitsch you prefer—the art of the grind­house and sen­sa­tion­al­ist dri­ve-in exploita­tion film? Or 20s silent avant-garde, the cool noir of the 30s and 40s, 50s B‑grade sci-fi, 60s psy­che­delia and French New Wave, or 80s pop­corn flicks…? What­ev­er kind of cin­e­ma grabs your atten­tion prob­a­bly first grabbed your atten­tion through the design of the movie poster, a genre that gets its due in nov­el­ty shops and spe­cial­ist exhi­bi­tions, but often goes unher­ald­ed in pop­u­lar con­cep­tions of art.

Despite its util­i­tar­i­an and unabashed­ly com­mer­cial func­tion, the movie poster can just as well be a work of art as any oth­er form. Fail­ing that, movie posters are at least always essen­tial archival arti­facts, snap­shots of the weird col­lec­tive uncon­scious of mass cul­ture: from Saul and Elaine Bass’ min­i­mal­ist poster for West Side Sto­ry (1961), “with its bright orange-red back­ground over the title with a sil­hou­ette of a fire escape with dancers” to more com­plex tableaux, like the bald­ly neo-impe­ri­al­ist Africa Texas Style! (1967), “which fea­tures a real­is­tic image of the pro­tag­o­nist on a horse, las­so­ing a zebra in front of a stam­pede of wilde­beest, ele­phants, and giraffes.”

These two descrip­tions only hint at the range of posters archived at the Uni­ver­si­ty of Texas Har­ry Ran­som Cen­ter—upwards of 5,000 in all, “from when the film indus­try was just begin­ning to com­pete with vaude­ville acts in the 1920s to the rise of the mod­ern megaplex and dri­ve-in the­aters in the 1970s.” So wrote Erin Willard in the Ran­som Center’s 2018 announce­ment of the dig­i­ti­za­tion of its mas­sive col­lec­tion. Thou­sands of posters have been pho­tographed and are avail­able online, down­load­able in “Large” and “Extra Large” res­o­lu­tions.

The bulk of the col­lec­tion comes from the Inter­state The­ater Circuit—a chain that, at one time, “con­sist­ed of almost every movie the­ater in Texas”—and encom­pass­es not only posters but film stills, lob­by cards, and press books from “the 1940s through the 1970s with a par­tic­u­lar strength in the films of the 1950s and 60s, includ­ing musi­cals, epics, west­erns, sword and san­dal, hor­ror, and counter cul­ture films.” Oth­er indi­vid­ual col­lec­tors have made siz­able dona­tions of their posters to the cen­ter, and the result is a tour of the many spec­ta­cles avail­able to the mid-cen­tu­ry Amer­i­can mind: lurid, vio­lent excess­es, maudlin mor­al­iz­ing, bizarre erot­ic fan­tasies, dime-store ado­les­cent adven­tures.…

Some of the films are well-known exam­ples from the peri­od; most of them are not, and there­in lies the thrill of brows­ing this online repos­i­to­ry, dis­cov­er­ing obscure odd­i­ties like the 1956 film Bare­foot Bat­tal­ion, in which “teen-age wolf packs become heroes in a nation’s fight for free­dom!” The num­ber of quirks and kinks on dis­play offers us a pruri­ent view of a decade too often flat­ly char­ac­ter­ized by its pen­chant for gray flan­nel suits. The Mad Men era was a peri­od of insti­tu­tion­al repres­sion and ram­pant sex­u­al harass­ment, not unlike our own time. It was also a lab­o­ra­to­ry for a libidi­nous anar­chy that threat­ened to unleash the pent-up ener­gy and cul­tur­al anx­i­ety of mil­lions of frus­trat­ed teenagers onto the world at large, as would hap­pen in the decades to come.

What we see in the mar­ket­ing of films like Five Brand­ed Women (1960) will vary wide­ly depend­ing on our ori­en­ta­tions and polit­i­cal sen­si­bil­i­ties. Is this cheap exploita­tion or an empow­er­ing pre­cur­sor to Mad Max: Fury Road? Maybe both. For cul­tur­al the­o­rists and film his­to­ri­ans, these pulpy adver­tise­ments offer win­dows into the psy­ches of their audi­ences and the film­mak­ers and pro­duc­tion com­pa­nies who gave them what they sup­pos­ed­ly want­ed. For the ordi­nary film buff, the Ran­som Cen­ter col­lec­tion offers eye can­dy of all sorts, and if they hap­pen to own a high-qual­i­ty print­er, the chance to hang posters on their wall that they prob­a­bly won’t see any­where else. Enter the online col­lec­tion here.

Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2018.

title: Brussels' Grand-Place Is Carpeted with 750,000 Fresh Dahlias in a Tribute to Hokusai
description: In Brussels’ iconic Grand-Place, a summer tradition literally blossoms in monumental style. The city’s Flower Carpet event, which this year celebr
body:
In Brussels’ iconic Grand-Place, a summer tradition literally blossoms in monumental style. The city’s Flower Carpet event, which this year celebrated its 24th edition, celebrates art, community, and diplomacy in the heart of Belgium’s capital, which is also the hub of the European Union. From August 13 to 16, the event marked 160 years of friendship between the nation and Japan, inviting artist Hiro Sugiyama to design a city square-sized composition, which he conceived as a tribute to ukiyo-e artist Katsushika Hokusai.
Titled “Neo Hokusai,” the monumental arrangement comprised more than 750,000 fresh dahlias, covering nearly 14,000 square feet. Framed with ornate patterns, the reimagining of the famous woodblock print “The Great Wave Off Kanagawa,” from Hokusai’s series Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji (1830-1832), glows in bright magenta, vermilion, and yellow. Flowers covered about 80 percent of the entire design.

Dahlias aren’t the only species artists choose to use for the carpet, although the 2024 edition also incorporated the voluminous blossoms. In 2018, a design highlighting the central Mexican region of Guanajuato grew out of one million begonias and was captured in an aerial timelapse by Joerg Daiber.
This year, the dahlias are sourced in partnership with Bloemencorso Loenhout, a giant flower parade that has been running for three quarters of a century in the northern city of Loenhout. This year, the event kicks off on September 12.

title: Glowing Paintings by Francesco Pirazzi Meditate on the Enigmas of Absence
description: “For me, paintings represent an attempt (sometimes more successful, sometimes less so) to grasp a ‘something’ that for some reason deeply moves me
body:
“For me, paintings represent an attempt (sometimes more successful, sometimes less so) to grasp a ‘something’ that for some reason deeply moves me, agitates me,” says Turin-based artist Francesco Pirazzi. In atmospheric, dreamlike paintings, deceptively simple architecture, trees, walkways, and other features of the landscape glow amid uncanny lighting.
“What drives my research is the feeling that something in reality is slightly off, that before my eyes lies an indecipherable enigma,” Pirazzi says, adding that he enjoys the way painting can encompass both reality and the “unknowable world,” and the ways they irresistibly converge. Deep shadows, minimalist archways, luminescent clouds, and exaggerated perspective combine in bold chromatic tableaux. “The subjects are recurring: trees, street lamps, houses, windows, hedges, and a few others that I feel I use as actors on a stage, each aware of their role,” Pirazzi says.
“Momenti” (2024), oil on linen, 70 x 80 centimeters
Light plays a unique role, establishing the mood and drawing our attention to what the artist describes as “the hierarchies between elements and the relationships that intertwine them, the things we must pay attention immediately to and those that need to emerge very slowly.” Illumination also reveals absence, which Pirazzi centers as much as the structures, plants, fences, and other objects. He’s interested in the unseen on the same level as what is visible, drawing us to these obscure and mysterious details.
Starting October 28, the artist’s work will be on view at Luce Gallery in Turin. See more on Pirazzi’s Instagram.

title: Dark Emotions Evoke Growth in Alejandro Aguliar Canela's Graphite Drawings
description: Alejandro Aguilar Canela finds profound value in what may be seen as some of our bleakest emotions. Delving into subject matters such as depressio
body:
Alejandro Aguilar Canela finds profound value in what may be seen as some of our bleakest emotions. Delving into subject matters such as depression, anger, abandonment, fear, individuality, sexuality, and more, Canela strives to understand the multitudes within each, and how their shadowy paths have the ability lead us somewhere brighter.
Though occasionally venturing into sculpture, the Austin, Texas-based artist specializes in drawing. His works range in size, with many of his compositions spanning two to four feet wide on both traditional paper and vellum. Canela largely employs graphite and fine line mechanical pencil, welcoming “mistakes” or inadvertent motifs—such as smudges and unplanned marks—that mirror his personal philosophy of embracing adverse emotions. 
“If I Could Protect You” (2024), mechanical pencil on paper, 14.3 x 14.4 inches
“There is another side to our own darkness, one that can reveal new perspectives and accelerate personal transformation,” the artist says. “It’s more about not discarding what might be considered unwanted, but instead finding some use for it.” As a result, these innermost feelings often manifest through unique characters, as Canela creates human-like forms to give them shape.
Several of Canela’s works are included in this year’s Critic’s Choice exhibition at Ki Smith Gallery in New York, which is on view through September 6. Find more from the artist on Instagram.
